items.stem: Which part of a plant takes in water from the soil?
options: The stem
The leaves
The flowers
The roots

explain.why: The stem carries water upwards, but it does not take water in from the soil; the roots do.
The leaves are above the ground. They lose water vapour to the air; they do not take water in from the soil.
Flowers help the plant to make seeds. They do not take water in from the soil.

solution: The roots grow in the soil and take in water and mineral salts from it.

items.stem: What is the job of the root hairs of a plant?
options: They make food for the plant.
They carry food from the leaves to the stem.
They take in water and mineral salts.
They let water vapour escape into the air.

explain.why: Food is made in the leaves, not in the root hairs.
Carrying food is the job of the food-carrying tubes. Root hairs take in water.
Water vapour is lost mainly from the leaves. Root hairs take water in.

solution: Root hairs are tiny growths on the roots. They take in water and mineral salts from the soil.

figure.alt: A young root with many tiny thread-like growths along it.

items.stem: A root has a great many very thin root hairs. How does this help the plant?
options: The root can make more food for the plant.
The root has a larger surface to take in water.
The leaves can take in more light.
The stem can carry food down faster.

explain.why: Roots do not make food. Food is made in the leaves.
Root hairs are underground and have nothing to do with light for the leaves.
Food is carried by the food-carrying tubes. Root hairs take in water.

solution: Many thin root hairs give the root a large surface, so more water and mineral salts can be taken in.

figure.alt: A young root with many tiny thread-like growths along it.

items.stem: The water-carrying tubes carry water from the ____ to the ____ of a plant.
options: leaves; roots
roots; leaves
flowers; stem
stem; roots

explain.why: Water moves up, from the roots to the leaves, not down from the leaves.
Water is taken in by the roots, not the flowers, so it does not start there.
Water does not move down to the roots. It moves up from them.

solution: Water is taken in by the roots and carried up the stem to the leaves by the water-carrying tubes.

items.stem: What do the food-carrying tubes of a plant carry?
options: Water taken in by the root hairs
Light energy from the Sun
Food made in the leaves
Water vapour lost from the leaves

explain.why: Water taken in by the root hairs is carried by the water-carrying tubes.
Plants take in light at the leaves. Tubes do not carry light.
Water vapour goes out into the air. The food-carrying tubes carry food.

solution: The leaves make food. The food-carrying tubes carry it to the other parts of the plant.

items.stem: How does the stem help a plant?
options: It takes in water from the soil for the plant.
It makes food for the whole plant to use.
It holds up the leaves and carries water and food.
It carries water but has no tubes for food.

explain.why: Water is taken in by the root hairs. The stem carries it up.
Food is made mainly in the leaves.
The stem has food-carrying tubes as well as water-carrying tubes.

solution: The stem supports the leaves and flowers. It also holds the water-carrying tubes and the food-carrying tubes.

items.stem: A celery stalk with leaves stands in coloured water for some hours. The veins of the leaves turn the same colour. What does this show?
options: Food moves down the stalk from the leaves.
The leaves took in the coloured water from the air.
The stalk made the colour by itself.
Water moves up the stalk to the leaves.

explain.why: Coloured water in the leaf veins came up from the beaker. It does not show food moving down.
The colour came from the beaker at the bottom of the stalk, not from the air.
The colour came from the water in the beaker.

solution: The coloured water reached the leaf veins by moving up through the stalk's water-carrying tubes.

figure.alt: A celery stalk with leaves standing in a beaker of coloured water.

items.stem: In which part of a plant is most of its food made?
options: The leaves
The roots
The stem
The flowers

explain.why: Roots take in water and mineral salts. They do not make food.
The stem carries food and water. Most food is made in the leaves.
Flowers help make seeds. Most food is made in the leaves.

solution: The leaves make most of the plant's food.

items.stem: In which direction does water move through a plant?
options: From the leaves down to the roots
Both up and down at the same time
Only sideways across the stem
From the roots up to the leaves

explain.why: Water is taken in at the roots and moves up. It does not move down to them.
The water-carrying tubes carry water in one direction only: up.
Water moves along the stem, from the roots to the leaves, not across it.

solution: The water-carrying tubes carry water from the roots up the stem to the leaves.

items.stem: Where does the food made in the leaves go?
options: To all parts of the plant
Only to the roots of the plant
Only to the flowers and fruits
Nowhere, because the leaves keep it all

explain.why: Food goes to every part of the plant, not just the roots.
Roots and stem also need food, so food goes to them too.
The food-carrying tubes carry the food away from the leaves to other parts.

solution: The food-carrying tubes take food from the leaves to all other parts of the plant.

items.stem: Why does a plant need water-carrying tubes in its stem?
options: So that food from the leaves can reach the roots
So that water from the roots can reach the leaves
So that the stem can take in water from the air
So that the stem can make food for the roots

explain.why: Carrying food is done by the food-carrying tubes.
The stem does not take water from the air. Water comes up from the roots.
The stem does not make the food. The leaves do.

solution: The roots take in water far below the leaves, so water-carrying tubes are needed to bring it up to them.

items.stem: Besides water, what else do the water-carrying tubes carry up from the roots?
options: Mineral salts
Food made in the roots
Light from the Sun
Water vapour

explain.why: Roots do not make food. The leaves make food.
Light is not carried in tubes. The leaves take it in.
Water vapour is lost from the leaves into the air. It is not carried up.

solution: The root hairs take in water and mineral salts together. Both are carried up by the water-carrying tubes.

options: Root hairs: make food; leaves: take in water
Root hairs: carry food; leaves: carry water
Stem: takes in water; root hairs: hold up the leaves
Root hairs: take in water; leaves: make food

The food-carrying tubes in the stem
The root hairs
The flowers

Root hairs take in water. They do not carry food.
Flowers do not carry food to the roots.

solution: The food-carrying tubes in the stem carry food made in the leaves down to the roots and to other parts.

In the roots
Evenly along the whole stem
Just above the ring

The food cannot get past the ring, so it does not reach the roots.
The ring blocks the food, so it builds up on one side only: above the ring.

solution: Food moves down from the leaves. It is stopped at the ring and collects just above it.

Tiny leaves

options: The food-carrying tubes have stopped carrying food to the roots.
The leaves are taking in too much water through their surface.
The stem has made too much food for the leaves.
The roots cannot take in enough water from the dry soil.

The leaves are losing water, not taking in too much.
The stem does not make food, and food is not the reason for drooping.

Root hairs
Air spaces in the stem

options: B, because it has no leaves to use up the water
Both the same, because water moves up at a fixed speed
B, because its food-carrying tubes are not blocked
A, because its leaves lose water, so more water is pulled up

explain.why: Leaves lose water to the air, and this pulls water up. Without leaves the water rises more slowly.
The speed depends on how much water the leaves lose, so the two are not the same.
Red ink travels in the water-carrying tubes, and leaves do not block them.

solution: Leaves lose water vapour. More water then moves up the stem to take its place, so the red ink rises higher in A.

Both parts, equally
Neither part

explain.why: Food from the leaves cannot pass down below the ring, so the lower part does not swell.
The ring blocks food from moving down, so only the upper part collects it.
Food collects above the ring, so that part swells.

solution: Food from the leaves is carried down. The ring stops it, so it collects above the ring and the stem swells there.

The leaves and the stem above the ring (A and B)

The leaves make food, so they do not starve. The parts below the ring do.
The parts above the ring still get food. It is the parts below the ring that do not.

solution: Food moves down from the leaves and is stopped by the ring, so only the stem below the ring and the roots miss out.

options: More water can now go up to the fruits on that branch.
Food from the leaves stays in the branch to feed the fruits.
The leaves make more food after the bark is removed.
The roots send extra food up the stem to the fruits.

explain.why: The ring only cuts the food-carrying tubes. Water movement is not changed.
The leaves make the same amount of food. The difference is where the food goes.
Roots do not make food. Food comes from the leaves.

solution: The ring stops the food from moving down, so more food stays in the branch and the fruits grow bigger.

items.stem: A ring of bark is removed from a stem. For a few days the leaves above the ring stay green and fresh. Why?
options: The water-carrying tubes still carry water up to them.
The food-carrying tubes can still bring food up to them.
The leaves can take in water from the air.
The bark has stored water for the leaves.

explain.why: The ring cut the food-carrying tubes. Water reaches the leaves in the water-carrying tubes.
Leaves lose water vapour. The water they need comes up the stem.
The leaves are kept fresh by water moving up the inner part, not by water stored in bark.

solution: Removing bark cuts only the food-carrying tubes. The water-carrying tubes are deeper inside, so water still reaches the leaves.

items.stem: A gardener digs up a small plant and many of its fine roots are torn off. After replanting, its leaves droop. Why?
options: Its food-carrying tubes have been blocked by soil in the new pot.
Its leaves can no longer make any food for the plant to use.
Fewer root hairs take in water, so less water reaches the leaves.
Its stem has begun to take in water instead of the roots.

explain.why: Food-carrying tubes are not what bring water to the leaves.
The drooping is from lack of water, which comes from the roots.
The stem does not take in water from soil. That is the job of the roots.

solution: Torn roots mean fewer root hairs, so less water enters. Less water goes up to the leaves, which droop.

items.stem: Cylinders P and Q each hold 100 mL of water with a layer of oil on top. A plant stem with leaves stands in P. A stem with no leaves stands in Q. Why was oil added to the water?
options: To stop water evaporating from the water surface
To give the plant extra food while it grows
To make the stem take in water much faster
To keep the leaves from losing water to the air

explain.why: Oil is not food for the plant. It is used only to cover the water.
The oil does not change how fast the stem takes in water.
The oil is on the water in the cylinder, not on the leaves.

solution: The oil covers the water, so any fall in water level is due to the plant and not to evaporation from the surface.

A stem without leaves takes in no water at all.

Leaves take in water from the air and drip it into P.

Both lose the same amount, because jelly is only on the surface
B, because water vapour can leave its leaves freely
A, because its roots take in more water

explain.why: Jelly covers the leaf and keeps the water in. It does not pull water out.
The jelly blocks water vapour at the surface, so A loses less.
Jelly on the leaves does not make the roots take in more water.

solution: The jelly stops water vapour leaving the leaves of A, so B loses more water.

options: Water moves up the inner stem to the leaves.
Food moves down through the outer part of the stem.
The red ink was made by the leaf veins.
Only roots carry water in a plant.

explain.why: Red ink travels in water. It does not show how food moves.
The ink was in the beaker. It was carried up to the leaves.
The inner stem and the leaf veins also turned red, so they carry water too.

solution: Red appears in the roots, then the inner stem and the leaf veins, but not the outer bark, so water moves up inside the stem to the leaves.

All the parts at the same time

Water cannot pass the ring, so the leaves soon droop.
Food can now move only upwards, towards the leaves.
Food can still pass down the strip, so the plant survives.

explain.why: The strip contains food-carrying tubes, so food can still pass.
Water travels in the inner part, which is not cut.
Food still moves down through the strip.

solution: Food-carrying tubes in the bark strip still carry food past the cut, so the roots keep getting food.

items.stem: Which set-up shows that water moves up the stem of a plant?
options: A ring of bark is removed from a stem, then the stem is observed.
A plant is placed in the dark for a few days.
The leaves of a plant are covered with petroleum jelly.
A cut stalk stands in red ink, then is cut across after some hours.

explain.why: This shows where food collects, not how water moves.
This does not test how water moves in the stem.
This tests water loss from leaves, not water moving up the stem.

solution: Red ink in the water shows where the water goes. Cutting the stalk across then shows red in the water-carrying tubes.

items.stem: Which set-up shows that food moves down a stem?
options: A stem is placed in red ink and cut across.
The roots of a plant are cut off and the plant is watched.
The stem of a plant is wrapped with a cloth for a week.
A ring of bark is removed and the stem is observed.

explain.why: This shows how water moves, not food.
This shows the roots take in water, not food moving down.
Wrapping a stem does not show which way food moves.

solution: When the bark is ringed, food collects above the ring. This shows food is moving down the stem.

items.stem: A student splits a celery stalk lengthwise after it has stood in red ink. Red lines run along the length of the stalk. What does this show?
options: The water-carrying tubes run along the stalk.
The food-carrying tubes are the red lines.
The red ink has made new tubes in the stalk.
The tubes run across the stalk, not along it.

explain.why: The red ink was in water, so the red lines mark the water-carrying tubes.
The tubes were already there. The ink just shows where they are.
The red lines run along the length, so the tubes do too.

solution: The red lines show tubes that carry water up. They run along the whole stalk.

items.stem: A branch is cut from a tree and left on the table. After a day its leaves have wilted, though they were fresh on the tree. Why?
options: The food-carrying tubes have stopped working.
The leaves have taken in too much water.
The stem has made too little food for the leaves.
Water lost by the leaves is no longer replaced.

explain.why: The leaves wilted because they lost water that was not replaced.
The leaves lost water. They did not take in too much.
The stem does not make food for the leaves. The leaves wilt because of lack of water.

solution: The leaves keep losing water vapour, but the cut branch has no roots to replace it, so the leaves wilt.

items.stem: The bar chart shows the water lost in one day by plants with different numbers of leaves. What does the chart show?
options: The more leaves a plant has, the less water it loses.
The number of leaves has no effect on water loss.
The more leaves a plant has, the more water it loses.
Plants with no leaves lose the most water.

explain.why: The bars get taller as leaves increase, so water loss increases.
The bars are different heights, so the number of leaves does matter.
The plant with no leaves has the shortest bar.

solution: The bars rise as the number of leaves increases, so more leaves means more water lost.

items.stem: A farmer adds mineral salts to the soil. Which parts of the plant bring the mineral salts to the leaves?
options: Root hairs and water-carrying tubes
Root hairs and food-carrying tubes
Leaves and water-carrying tubes
Leaves and food-carrying tubes

explain.why: Mineral salts go up with water, in the water-carrying tubes.
Leaves do not take in mineral salts from the soil.
Leaves do not take them in, and food-carrying tubes carry food.

solution: Root hairs take in the mineral salts. The water-carrying tubes carry them to the leaves.

items.stem: A ring of bark is removed near the base of a tree trunk. After many months the whole tree dies. What is the best explanation?
options: The water-carrying tubes were removed, so no water reaches the leaves.
The roots get no food, die, and can no longer take in water.
The leaves can no longer make food without bark.
The roots have too much food and are damaged.

explain.why: Only the food-carrying tubes were cut. Water carries on moving up for a while.
The leaves can still make food. The problem is that it cannot reach the roots.
The roots get no food, not too much.

solution: Food cannot pass the ring to the roots. The roots starve and die, so no water can be taken in and the whole tree dies.

items.stem: Which pair of plant parts works together to bring water from the soil to the leaves?
options: Root hairs and food-carrying tubes
Leaves and water-carrying tubes
Root hairs and water-carrying tubes
Leaves and food-carrying tubes

explain.why: Water is not carried by the food-carrying tubes.
Leaves do not take in water from the soil.
Neither takes water from the soil to the leaves.

solution: The root hairs take in water and the water-carrying tubes carry it up to the leaves.

items.stem: Mei Ling wants to find out if leaves affect how much water a stem takes up. She uses a stem with 6 leaves and a stem with none. What is the one thing she changes?
options: The amount of water in each cylinder
The thickness of the stem
The layer of oil on the water
The number of leaves on the stem

explain.why: This should stay the same so that the test is fair.
The stems should be of the same thickness, so the test is fair.
Both cylinders should have the same oil, so only leaves differ.

solution: In a fair test only the thing being tested changes. Here it is the number of leaves.

items.stem: On a hot, dry day a plant's leaves lose water vapour faster than usual. What happens in the plant?
options: Water moves down the stem to the roots.
More water moves up the stem to the leaves.
The food-carrying tubes bring water to the leaves.
Nothing changes in the stem.

explain.why: Water moves up the stem, and moves faster when more is lost.
The water-carrying tubes bring water to the leaves.
More water is lost from the leaves, so more water is taken up to replace it.

solution: The leaves lose more water, so more water is pulled up through the water-carrying tubes to replace it.

items.stem: A leaf is cut from a plant, with its stalk placed in red ink. After some time its veins turn red. What does this show?
options: The leaf makes red food in its veins.
The leaf took in red ink through its flat surface.
The veins carry food only, not water.
Water-carrying tubes run into the leaf veins.

explain.why: The red came from the ink, not from food made by the leaf.
The ink was taken in at the stalk, and carried up to the veins.
The red veins show they carry water too.

solution: Red ink moved up the stalk and into the veins, so water-carrying tubes run into the leaf.

items.stem: Which part of a stem must be cut away to stop food reaching the roots but still let water reach the leaves?
options: A ring of the outer bark
The inner part where the red dots appear
The whole centre of the stem
The tip of the stem

explain.why: The inner dots are the water-carrying tubes. Cutting them stops water.
Cutting the centre would damage the water-carrying tubes.
This does not stop food passing down the stem.

solution: The food-carrying tubes are in the outer bark. A ring cut there stops food but leaves the water-carrying tubes.

items.stem: Stalks A and B stand in equal amounts of red ink in the same place. A has all its leaves and B has none. The graph shows how high the red ink rose in each. What does the graph show?
options: Leaves slow down the water moving up the stalk.
Water moves up only when the stalk has no leaves.
Leaves make the red ink, so the stalk is coloured.
Leaves make water move up the stalk faster.

explain.why: A, with leaves, has the steeper line, so water moves faster with leaves.
The red also rises in B, which has no leaves, but more slowly.
The red ink came from the beaker. The graph compares how fast it rises.

solution: A rises 4 cm each hour, and B only 2 cm. The stalk with leaves takes up water faster because the leaves lose water.

options: 16 cm
18 cm
10 cm
20 cm

explain.why: 16 cm is the height at 4 hours. A rises 4 cm more in the next hour.
A rises 4 cm each hour, not 2 cm, so the height is 20 cm.
10 cm uses the rate of stalk B (2 cm each hour). Stalk A rises 4 cm each hour.

solution: A rises 4 cm each hour, so after 5 hours it is 5 x 4 = 20 cm.

options: The ring let more water move to the mangoes.
The ring made the leaves on the branch make more food.
More food stayed in the ringed branch for its mangoes.
The roots sent more food up to the ringed branch.

explain.why: The ring cuts the food-carrying tubes, not the water-carrying tubes.
The ring does not change how much food the leaves make. It stops it going down.
Roots do not make food to send up.

solution: The ringed branch kept the food it made, so its mangoes became heavier.

items.stem: Cylinder A has a stem with leaves and oil on the water. B has a stem with leaves and no oil. C has a stem with no leaves and no oil. Which two should be compared to find how much water the leaves lose?
options: A and B
A and C
A, B and C together
B and C

explain.why: A and B differ in the oil, not the leaves, so they do not show the effect of leaves.
A and C differ in both leaves and oil, so the effect of leaves cannot be seen.
Using all three together does not give a fair comparison.

solution: B and C differ only in leaves. The extra water lost by B is the water lost by the leaves.

options: 3 mL
15 mL
12 mL
18 mL

explain.why: 3 mL is the water lost by C, which has no leaves.
15 mL is lost by B, but part of that is lost from the water surface.
18 mL adds the loss of B and C. To find the effect of leaves, subtract C from B.

solution: B lost 15 mL and C lost 3 mL, so the leaves lost 15 - 3 = 12 mL. A also lost 12 mL with oil covering the water.

items.stem: Three plants stand in the same place for six weeks. Plant P has a full ring of bark removed. Plant Q has a ring removed except for a narrow strip of bark. Plant R has no ring removed. P wilts and dies. Q and R stay healthy. What does this show?
options: A strip of bark can carry water in place of the water-carrying tubes.
Plants do not need food-carrying tubes.
A strip of bark is enough to carry food to the roots.
Only plants with no ring can survive.

explain.why: Bark carries food. Water travels in the tubes inside the stem.
P died because the food-carrying tubes were cut.
Q survived too, so a ring with a strip left does not kill the plant.

solution: Q survived because the strip still held food-carrying tubes, so food reached the roots. P's roots starved.

items.stem: Mr Lim removes a ring of bark near the base of a young tree. The tree looks healthy for a few weeks and then dies. Why does it not die at once?
options: The roots make their own food until the leaves wilt.
The food-carrying tubes below the ring bring food up from the soil.
The roots use up food stored earlier before it runs out.
The water-carrying tubes bring food down instead.

explain.why: Roots cannot make food. Food comes from the leaves.
Plants do not take food in from the soil, and the tubes carry food from the leaves.
Water-carrying tubes carry water up, not food down.

solution: The roots had stored food. They use it up first and die when it is gone. Then the tree dies too.

items.stem: A ring of bark is removed from a stem. The table shows the width of the stem measured above and below the ring at the start and after 8 weeks. What does the table show about food?
options: Food collected above the ring as it could not go down.
Food collected below the ring because it moved up.
Food moved evenly above and below the ring.
No food moved in the stem at all.

explain.why: The part below the ring did not get wider, so food did not collect there.
Only the part above the ring got wider.
The wider stem above the ring shows food collected there.

solution: The stem above the ring widened from 5 mm to 8 mm, so food collected there. Food could not pass the ring.

items.stem: A scientist blocks the water-carrying tubes at one point of a stem with wax, and leaves the bark alone. What happens to the leaves above that point?
options: They droop because water cannot pass the blocked point.
They stay fresh because the food-carrying tubes carry water.
They grow larger because food collects there.
They stay fresh because they take in water from the air.

explain.why: Food-carrying tubes do not carry water up.
Food collecting is the result of a ring in the bark, not wax in the inner tubes.
Leaves lose water. They do not take in water from the air.

solution: The wax blocks the water-carrying tubes. Water cannot get past it, so the leaves above lose water and droop.

items.stem: Plants S and T are the same kind and size, with the same number of leaves, in the same sunny place. S has dry soil and T has moist soil. Which droops first, and why?
options: S, because its roots cannot take in enough water
T, because its roots take in too much water from the soil
T, because its leaves lose water faster than S
Neither, because both have the same kind of leaves

explain.why: Plants with enough water do not droop. S has too little.
Both have the same leaves and place, so they lose about the same water.
The soil differs, so the water the roots can take in is different.

solution: Both lose similar amounts of water. Only S has too little water in the soil to replace it, so S droops first.

items.stem: The bar chart shows the water lost by a plant in three places in one day. Which statement is supported?
options: A plant loses the most water in a cool, still place.
A plant loses the most water in a hot, windy place.
A plant loses the same amount of water in all three places.
A plant takes in water faster in a cool place.

explain.why: The cool, still bar is the shortest, so the plant loses least there.
The bars are of different heights, so water loss is not the same.
The chart shows water lost, not water taken in.

solution: The hot, windy bar is the tallest, so most water is lost there.

items.stem: A plant is placed in red ink. Only the inner part of the stem turns red, and not the bark. Which is the best explanation?
options: The bark carries water, but too slowly to turn red.
The inner tubes carry food, and the bark tubes carry water.
The bark does not let colour in.
The inner tubes carry water, and the bark tubes carry food.

explain.why: The bark carries food. It is the inner tubes that carry the red water.
This is the wrong way round. The inner tubes carry water.
The red is carried inside the water-carrying tubes. The bark carries something else.

solution: Red ink moves in water, and it shows only in the water-carrying tubes of the inner stem. The bark carries food.

items.stem: Which observation best shows that water moves up a stem and not down?
options: Red ink shows low in a stalk first and higher up later.
The stem swells above a ring of bark that has been removed.
The leaves of a cut branch wilt after a day.
The soil in a pot gets drier after a day.

explain.why: This shows food moving down, not water.
This shows the leaves lose water, not which way water moves.
This does not show the direction of water in the stem.

solution: If water moves up, the red ink should be seen low in the stalk first and then higher.

items.stem: A ring of bark is removed from a branch, and then all the leaves above the ring are cut off. After some weeks the stem above the ring does not swell. Why?
options: The ring lets food pass down easily.
Water cannot move up past the ring.
No food is made above the ring, so none collects there.
The food-carrying tubes grow back above the ring.

explain.why: The ring blocks food. Here there is no food above the ring to block.
Water moves past the ring through the inner tubes.
No food is made, so there is nothing to collect above the ring.

solution: Food is made in the leaves. With the leaves gone there is no food to collect above the ring.

items.stem: A plant in a cylinder of water has oil on the water. The graph shows the total water lost over six days. At the end of day 3 something was done to the plant. What was done?
options: A ring of bark was removed from its stem.
Most of its leaves were removed.
The oil layer was taken off the water.
More leaves were added to the plant.

explain.why: A ring does not stop water moving up, so water loss would not slow so much.
Taking off the oil would let more water evaporate, so the line would be steeper.
More leaves would make the plant lose water faster, so the line would be steeper.

solution: The plant lost 8 mL a day until day 3, then only about 2 mL a day. Losing most leaves reduces water loss.

items.stem: A balsam stem stands in red ink for 20 minutes. It is then cut at three heights above the water, with the results shown. What does the table suggest?
options: There are no water-carrying tubes at 20 cm.
The red ink had not yet risen as far as 20 cm.
The food-carrying tubes end at 10 cm.
The red ink moves down from 20 cm to 2 cm.

explain.why: The tubes run all the way up, and the ink just had not reached 20 cm yet.
Red ink moves in water, so it does not show food-carrying tubes.
The red is found near the bottom, which shows it rises from there.

solution: The red was found at 2 cm and 10 cm but not at 20 cm, so after 20 minutes the ink had not reached 20 cm.

options: The jelly added extra water to the soil in pot A.
Plant A lost less water, so its roots took in less.
The jelly blocked the food-carrying tubes of A.
The leaves of A took in water from the soil.

explain.why: Jelly does not add water to the soil.
The jelly is on the leaves and blocks water vapour, not tubes.
Leaves do not take in water from the soil. Roots do.

solution: Jelly keeps water vapour in. Plant A needs to replace less water, so its roots take in less and the soil stays wetter.

items.stem: The table shows four rows about the tubes of a plant. Which row is correct?
options: B
C
D
A

explain.why: In B, the food-carrying tubes are said to carry water.
In C, food is said to move only from the leaves to the roots, and the water-carrying tubes are said to carry food.
In D, food is said to move only up from the roots.

solution: A is correct: water-carrying tubes carry water up from the roots, and food-carrying tubes carry food made in the leaves to all parts.

items.stem: Plant K has all its root hairs removed. Plant L has a ring of bark removed from its stem. Both stand in moist soil in the same place. Which droops first, and why?
options: K, because it cannot take in water
L, because the ring stops water moving up
L, because the ring stops its leaves making food
Both droop at the same time

explain.why: The ring cuts the food-carrying tubes. Water still moves up in L.
Leaves still make food. The ring affects where food goes.
L still takes in and carries water, so it does not droop soon.

solution: K has no root hairs, so water cannot enter and K droops first. L still gets water for a while.

items.stem: A ring of bark is removed from a stem. The plant then stands in red ink for 2 hours. Where will red be seen?
options: Only below the ring
In the inner stem and in the leaves above the ring
Nowhere above the ring, because the ink cannot pass it
Only in the bark above the ring

explain.why: Water moves past the ring through the inner tubes and into the leaves.
The ring cuts only the bark, so the red ink moves up in the inner tubes.
The bark carries food. The red is in the water-carrying tubes.

solution: The ring cuts the bark only. Red ink moves up the inner tubes and reaches the leaves.

items.stem: A student puts a stalk in red ink and sees red on its outside, from splashes. How can she show that the red was carried inside the stalk?
options: Cut the stalk across and look for red dots inside.
Measure the mass of the stalk after an hour.
Count the number of leaves on the stalk.
Look at the colour of the beaker.

explain.why: The mass does not show where the ink went.
The number of leaves does not show where the ink went.
The beaker's colour does not show what is inside the stalk.

solution: Red dots inside a cut stalk show that the ink travelled in its tubes.

items.stem: A ring of bark is removed from the base of a stem. Three statements are made. I: Water still moves up past the ring. II: Food collects above the ring. III: The roots will eventually die. Which are correct?
options: I, II and III
I and II only
II and III only
I and III only

explain.why: Statement III is also correct: the roots receive no food and die.
Statement I is also correct: the water-carrying tubes are not cut.
Statement II is also correct: food collects above the ring.

solution: The ring cuts only the food-carrying tubes. So water still moves up (I), food collects above (II), and the roots starve and die (III).

items.stem: Stalk A and stalk B both have leaves. A stands in red ink. B has a ring of bark removed and stands in red ink. C has leaves and stands in plain water. After two hours, which stalks have red-coloured veins in the leaves?
options: A only
A and B only
B only
A, B and C

explain.why: The ring cuts only the bark, so water still moves up in B, and its leaf veins turn red.
A has no ring, and red still reaches its leaves.
C is in plain water, so it takes up no red ink.

solution: A and B stand in red ink, and the ring in B does not block the water-carrying tubes. C has no ink, so none of C is red.

items.stem: Plant X has many root hairs. Plant Y has few root hairs. They are the same size and have the same leaves and soil. Which statement is correct?
options: Y can take in water faster, so it is less likely to droop.
X makes less food because it has many root hairs.
X can take in water faster, so it droops less.
X and Y take in the same amount of water.

explain.why: More root hairs mean a larger surface, so X takes in water faster.
Root hairs do not affect how much food the leaves make.
A plant with more root hairs takes in more water.

solution: More root hairs give a larger surface for taking in water, so X takes in more water.

items.stem: Which shows the path taken by food made in a leaf to a root?
options: Leaf, then the water-carrying tubes in the stem, then the roots
Leaf, then the food-carrying tubes in the stem, then the roots
Root hairs, then the food-carrying tubes, then the leaf
Leaf, then the root hairs, then the stem

explain.why: The water-carrying tubes carry water up, not food down.
This path goes from the roots to the leaf, the wrong way.
Food does not pass through the root hairs.

solution: Food made in the leaf travels down the stem in the food-carrying tubes to the roots.

items.stem: A tree is ringed between two side branches J and K, as shown. The roots get food only from leaves below the ring. Which statement is correct?
options: Food made in J cannot reach the roots, but food made in K can.
Food made in both J and K can reach the roots.
Food made in neither J nor K can reach the roots.
Food made in K cannot reach the roots, but food made in J can.

explain.why: K is above the ring, so its food is stopped there. J is below the ring.
Food from K must pass the ring, which stops it.
J is below the ring, so its food can still reach the roots.

solution: Food moves down. Food from K is stopped at the ring, while food from J starts below it and reaches the roots.

items.stem: Why does a leaf need both water-carrying tubes and food-carrying tubes?
options: Water-carrying tubes bring it food, and food-carrying tubes take away water.
Both tubes bring it water from the soil.
Water-carrying tubes bring it water, and food-carrying tubes take food away.
Both tubes take away the food the leaf makes.

explain.why: Water-carrying tubes bring water, and food-carrying tubes take food away.
Only the water-carrying tubes carry water.
Only the food-carrying tubes take food away.

solution: Water comes in through the water-carrying tubes, and the food made in the leaf leaves through the food-carrying tubes.

items.stem: Raj wants to compare how fast red ink rises in stalks of different kinds. What should he measure?
options: The mass of each beaker at the start of the test
The number of stalks standing in each beaker
The thickness of the leaves on each stalk
The height of the red mark in each stalk

explain.why: The beaker's mass does not show how far the ink rose.
The number of stalks does not show how far the ink rose.
Leaf thickness does not show how far the ink rose.

solution: Measuring the height of the red mark after the same time shows how fast the ink rose in each stalk.

items.stem: Two identical leafy stems stand in equal amounts of water. Stem P is in a warm, dry, windy place. Stem Q is in a cool, damp, still room. After a day, in which beaker has the water level fallen more?
options: The beaker with stem P, because its leaves lose more water into the air
The beaker with stem Q, because the water cannot evaporate from its leaves
Both beakers the same, because the stems are identical
The beaker with stem Q, because cool water travels up faster

explain.why: Damp, still air slows the loss of water from leaves, so stem Q takes up less water.
The stems are identical but the places are not. Warm, dry, windy air makes leaves lose water faster.
Water moves up because the leaves lose water, and cool damp air slows this.

solution: Warm, dry, windy air makes the leaves lose water faster.
The stem then takes up more water to replace it, so the water level falls more in beaker P.
